description: Cold Movers is building a public web tool for SPHEREx: enter sky coordinates and watch the region change over time as a movie, so anyone can spot what moves or varies. Our Madhava engine fits a band-integrated Planck curve to the 102 infrared bands to estimate each object's temperature and flag unusual spectra. Led by a precision machinist and materials researcher from Honduras. We welcome help with web development, data visualization, astrophysics, and video.
summary:
Cold Movers is a free web app that turns NASA's SPHEREx repeated infrared observations into a modern blink comparator, the digital version of how Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto. Type any coordinates or pick a challenge object: the app fetches the SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 images covering it from NASA/IPAC IRSA, aligns them and plays the sky visit by visit. It finds what moves without any catalogue, confirming motion only when two or more of SPHEREx's six simultaneous detectors agree, and fits a blackbody-equivalent temperature with our Madhava engine, a band-integrated Planck fit with a guaranteed bound on its series error. Explicit verdicts (CONFIRMED, CANDIDATE, INCONCLUSIVE) and a traffic light say when the data cannot support a conclusion. On the test objects it confirms the motion of Barnard's Star and Epsilon Indi B on its own, keeps WISE 0855 as a candidate, and claims no discovery. Its detection rates come only from artificial movers injected into real images and were checked on pre-registered held-out tests. It matters because students, citizen scientists and astronomers can explore SPHEREx from any phone and see honestly what the data can and cannot show.

Live app: https://cold-movers.streamlit.app
details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Cold Movers is a digital blink comparator for NASA's SPHEREx, inspired by the way Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930. For any coordinates, star name or challenge object it:

• asks NASA/IPAC IRSA for the SPHEREx images covering that spot (Data Release 1 + Quick Release 3) and downloads small cutouts;

• aligns them on one sky grid and stacks each detector's images per visit, so the sky can be played visit by visit (movie, difference and sum views);

• finds what moves with no catalogue at all: sources are followed through the visits and fitted with a straight line, and a motion is CONFIRMED only when two or more of SPHEREx's six simultaneously exposed detectors agree; otherwise it stays a CANDIDATE, or INCONCLUSIVE when the detectors cannot be trusted;

• measures the object's 0.75–5 µm spectrum and fits a blackbody-equivalent temperature with our Madhava engine: an exact band-integrated Planck fit whose series carries a guaranteed error bound, with a traffic light that says when the number cannot be trusted (saturation, too narrow a wavelength range, light that is not a single blackbody);

• explains every result in plain words and keeps the link to every original SPHEREx file.

RESULTS (tests on known objects, not discoveries)

• Barnard's Star: 9.83″/yr found with no catalogue (catalogue 10.39″/yr); trajectory fit 10.69 ± 0.76″/yr, 0.4σ from the catalogue. Epsilon Indi B: 4.54″/yr, confirmed by 5 detectors (catalogue 4.68″/yr). WISE 0855: only a candidate (one detector).

• TRAPPIST-1: blackbody-equivalent 2,464 K against a published effective temperature of 2,566 ± 26 K (−4 %, a different quantity). R Draconis seen to vary (0.57 mag, 9.6σ).

• Validation scoreboard with rules fixed in advance: 14 pass, 4 partial, 1 fail (very red movers seen by only two detectors). Detection rates come only from artificial movers injected into real SPHEREx images: in a pre-registered held-out test, precision 0.99 and recall 0.40 at S/N 15 on the six test fields, and recall 0.72 on two SPHEREx fields never used before.

• A pre-registered calibration found that some of our own error bars are too small (blind-search speed uncertainties, temperature intervals). We published that, as we promised before running it.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Citizen scientists, students and teachers can explore SPHEREx from any phone or computer, with no installation or account, and see a star move across the sky in one year. Astronomers get a quick, traceable first look at any position. Above all, the tool shows how to be honest with data: it separates real measurements from tests, and says "inconclusive" instead of inventing a number.

TOOLS

Python 3.12; Astropy, Astroquery and PyVO (IRSA, Gaia and SIMBAD access); NumPy and SciPy; Matplotlib, Pillow and Plotly; Streamlit (web app, hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud); GitHub and GitHub Actions (101 automated tests, a headless run of the whole app, reproduction of every published result and a robot that checks the live app after every app update). Data: SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 (NASA/IPAC IRSA), Gaia DR3, SIMBAD. No special hardware. AI assistance is declared in the Use of AI section.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

A 1930 discovery technique applied to a 2025 mission; confirmation by SPHEREx's own simultaneous detectors instead of a catalogue; an engine named after Madhava of Sangamagrama that, like him, corrects a truncated series instead of cutting it; and an evidence ledger that labels every result as a real measurement, an injection test, a candidate or an inconclusive result.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Stars too bright for SPHEREx (saturation), blended neighbours, objects too cold for SPHEREx to see their peak, parallax (at most 0.19″/yr of bias on these objects), the difference between blackbody-equivalent and effective temperature, outages of the archive services (precomputed results and time limits keep the app working), reproducibility (fixed seeds, pinned libraries, pre-registered tests), accessibility (plain words, phone layout) and credits for every data source. Not an official NASA product.
